The Bantu expansion was the slow spread of Bantu-speaking farming peoples from West-Central Africa, around the border of Nigeria and Cameroon, across most of Africa south of the equator. It took thousands of years, and its dates are broad estimates; linguists place its start as early as about 4000 BCE, and it reached the far south by around 500 CE.

The main evidence is language. Some 500 Bantu languages, including Swahili, Zulu, Kikongo, Shona and Kinyarwanda, are spoken over a huge area and are closely related, a sign that their speakers spread from one place not very long ago. Genetic studies agree.

The spread seems to have taken two main paths:

  • West, south through or around the Congo rainforest, reaching what is now Angola around 500 BCE.
  • East, along the northern edge of the forest to the Great Lakes region, then south down East Africa.

The newcomers brought farming, pottery and, from the first millennium BCE, iron working, part of the story of iron metallurgy in Africa. They grew yams and oil palm, and later took up sorghum, millets and cattle from the savanna peoples they met, and bananas that had come from Southeast Asia. They absorbed, displaced or lived alongside earlier hunter-gatherers and herders, such as the forest peoples of central Africa and the Khoisan of the south.

Almost everything later in the history of central, eastern and southern Africa grew from this movement. The kingdoms of the Congo basin, the states of the Great Lakes, Great Zimbabwe and the Swahili city-states of the coast were all built by Bantu-speaking peoples. Today hundreds of millions of Africans speak a Bantu language.
